newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila says banking on U.S. help in Spratlys.
newsitem.headline: Manila says banking on U.S. help in Spratlys.

text.p: The Philippines' military chief on Monday said China risked being branded a bully over its behaviour in the contested Spratly Islands and urged Washington to be ready to deal with any trouble in the potentially oil-rich area.

"The possibility is there, that's why it's called a 'flashpoint'," General Arnulfo Acedera told reporters when asked about the danger of an armed confrontation among rival claimants to the Spratlys and adjacent islands.
"China will be up against world opinion if they bully their way around," he said.

Beijing has insisted the Spratlys and other islands in the South China Sea historically belongs to China. The Spratlys are also being claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.
Manila and Beijing are also disputing ownership of Scarborough Shoal, a 16-km (10-mile) rock formation 200 km (125 miles) off the Philippines' Subic freeport.

Acedera proposed "insertion of do-able or implementable contingency plans" in the mutual defence treaty between the Philippines and the United States to deal with any emergency in the South China Sea arising from the territorial disputes.
The treaty, which calls on both countries to aid each other in case of an attack on the other, allows for the adoption of such plans, he said.
American diplomats have said the treaty does not cover contested territories.
Relations between Manila and Beijing have been marred by diplomatic clashes over the Spratlys and Scarborough Shoal.
The Philippines accused China in April of sending armed naval ships near islands in the Spratlys claimed by Manila but Beijing said they were research vessels on a scientific mission.
Last week, Beijing accused Manila of violating Chinese sovereignty after Filipino fishermen hoisted a flag over the shoal.
In a move that analysts said could further incense China, a group of congressmen sailed to the shoal last weekend and asserted Philippine sovereignty over the area.
The Chinese embassy, asked about the Filipinos' trip, said only that Beijing's statement last week "remains valid".

Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon told reporters Manila would explain to Beijing that the legislators' trip was not officially sanctioned and that in a democracy, it was expected that some individual Filipinos would express their views.
